title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT (two January 2023 versions) and GPT-4, focusing on whether these large language models can serve as useful assistants for mathematical work. Rather than studying classroom learning outcomes, the authors benchmark the models on a newly created dataset, GHOSTS, and a smaller subset, miniGHOSTS, designed to probe different dimensions of mathematical reasoning such as factual recall, proof completion, theorem proving, symbolic integration, olympiad-style problem solving, and search/definition retrieval.

The intervention studied is not an educational treatment but the use of ChatGPT/GPT-4 as a mathematical assistant. The paper uses prompts drawn from graduate- and undergraduate-level textbooks, math.stackexchange, the MATH dataset, and hand-crafted problems, and evaluates model outputs with manually assigned ratings, error codes, and warning codes. The paper’s context is advanced mathematics rather than school mathematics; the most relevant human populations are undergraduate and graduate-level mathematical users, not K-12 learners.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is most useful as a factual lookup or search-style assistant, but performs inconsistently on deeper mathematical reasoning and generally falls below the level needed for reliable graduate-level mathematics. GPT-4 improves performance substantially and can handle many undergraduate-level questions better than ChatGPT, but still struggles with graduate-level difficulty and proof-heavy tasks. The paper therefore positions these models as helpful support tools for mathematically proficient users, not as dependable solvers for advanced mathematical problems.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style benchmark study with a clear manual evaluation protocol, but it is not an intervention study in K-12 education and does not use an experimental or causal design. The evidence is observational/analytical and focused on model capability assessment rather than learner outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no educational impact on student achievement in middle school mathematics; it evaluates LLM performance on advanced mathematics benchmarks and assistant utility for mathematicians. Any relevance to middle school math is indirect and the reported results suggest limited reliability for more complex tasks.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT versions and GPT-4 as mathematical assistants for advanced math tasks, including proof completion, theorem/fact retrieval, symbolic integration, and solving undergraduate/graduate-level exercises.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not study student learning; it benchmarks ChatGPT (9-Jan and 30-Jan 2023) and GPT-4 on natural-language mathematics tasks. Performance was mixed and generally below graduate level: 9-Jan ChatGPT averaged 3.20/5 (SD=1.23) on GHOSTS, 30-Jan ChatGPT averaged 3.29/5 (SD=1.28), and GPT-4 averaged 4.15/5 (SD=1.12) on miniGHOSTS, with stronger results on fact retrieval than on proof-based or graduate-level tasks.
finding.measure: Human-rated correctness/performance on math benchmark prompts (rating 1-5), including GHOSTS and miniGHOSTS subdatasets
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts total in GHOSTS; n=170 prompts in miniGHOSTS for GPT-4

finding.finding_summary: The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be useful as a mathematical assistant for querying facts, acting as a search engine or knowledge-base interface, and speeding up lookup tasks in a mathematician’s workflow. This is a qualitative efficiency finding rather than a learning outcome, with no experimental effect size reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of usefulness for fact querying, definition retrieval, theorem naming, and proof-outline retrieval
